title: 188,000 Left in a Few Hours. Then They Were Ordered to Pay the State.
title_candidates: 188,000 Left in a Few Hours. Then They Were Ordered to Pay the State.
A County Left on an Order. The Only Court That Looked Could Not Say Who Was Ordered.
description:
On the twelfth of February 2017, the emergency spillway at the Oroville Dam in northern California was failing, and 188,000 people were ordered out of their homes. They left within a few hours. Two days later they were allowed back.

The dam held. This film is about what happened to the two days.

Four of those people — Francis Bechtel, Jacob Klein, Chantel Ramirez and Denise Johnson — asked the State of California to pay back what the evacuation had cost them: the out-of-pocket expenses of two days, and the loss of the use of their homes for two days. They asked on behalf of everybody who had been ordered out.

The case turned on a question nobody expects. An evacuation order is written to be obeyed in the hour it is given, not to be proved in a courtroom five years later, and the order that emptied the county did not name a boundary anyone could later draw. So when the court came to ask who exactly had been ordered to leave, the answer, in the only court that ever looked at it, was that it cannot be established.

The four were ordered to pay the State's costs of the appeal in which that was decided.

Every quotation on screen is from the record: the opinion of the California Court of Appeal, Third Appellate District, of 15 March 2022, and the trial court's ruling as the appeal court quotes it.

This is general history, not legal advice. Some imagery is AI-assisted and symbolic — a reconstruction, not authentic footage, and no real person's likeness is depicted.
